WBM AET: Oudin vs. Penman-Monteith, validated against OpenET and flux towers

National Park Service Water Balance Model · generated July 27, 2026

This report compares two ways of driving potential evapotranspiration (PET) in the NPS Water Balance Model (WBM) — the default Oudin method and FAO-56 Penman-Monteith — against two independent references: OpenET (satellite-based remote-sensing ET) and eddy-covariance flux tower ET, across 35 sites spanning five ecosystem types and a wide elevation and climate gradient (2016–2023).

Headline result: uncalibrated, Penman-Monteith AET tracks both OpenET and flux tower ET noticeably better than the default Oudin run — lower RMSE, less negative bias, and a regression slope closer to 1 across nearly every comparison.

Methods

The WBM is a daily rain/snow/snowmelt/soil-moisture/AET/runoff model. Both PET methods were run with identical snow, soil, and runoff parameters, so any difference in AET is attributable to the PET method alone. Oudin PET is a temperature-only formulation with a topographic heat-load/shade adjustment. Penman-Monteith is a full energy-balance method that additionally requires humidity and wind; it returns a reference-grass ET (ETo) rather than PET directly, so it was converted with a crop coefficient of Kc = 1.0 (a simplifying baseline — see the repo's notebook 06 for detail). Wind was sourced from gridMET (10 m) and corrected to the 2 m height FAO-56 assumes. Neither run is calibrated against OpenET or flux tower ET; this is a head-to-head comparison of the two PET methods as-is. WBM AET is compared to OpenET's 4 km grid-cell-averaged ensemble (matching the WBM's own gridMET resolution) and, separately, to each site's own flux-tower ET.

Where does each method do better? (spatial view)

Mapping the per-site difference in RMSE vs. OpenET (RMSE(Penman-Monteith) − RMSE(Oudin)) shows Penman-Monteith winning (blue) at most sites, including the largest margins in the Northern Rockies and Sierra Nevada — with Oudin holding a slight edge (red) mainly in drier Southwest shrubland/grassland sites.

Penman-Monteith's advantage is largest in Croplands, Evergreen Forests, and Grasslands. Oudin holds a small edge in Shrublands and Wetland/Riparian sites — both arid or sparsely-vegetated settings where the Kc = 1.0 baseline may overstate Penman-Monteith's reference-ET-to-PET conversion.

Takeaways

Even without any calibration, Penman-Monteith produces a materially better match to both independent ET references than the temperature-only Oudin method — likely because it captures more of the energy balance (radiation, humidity, wind) that drives real ET variability, rather than temperature alone. That said, both methods still underestimate AET on average (negative mean bias) and both show negative mean R² overall, driven by a handful of poor-performing sites (e.g. wetland/riparian sites with unusually high observed ET) — so neither is calibration-ready as-is. The most promising next step is applying the same PET-multiplier calibration already built for Oudin (repo notebook 04) to the Penman-Monteith run, and testing an ecosystem-specific Kc in place of the 1.0 baseline, particularly for the shrubland/wetland sites where Oudin currently holds a slight edge.
